title: Bertrand’s box
objectives: Count the faces, not the boxes, to find the chance the hidden side matches.
Check the count with a tree and with odds form.
See that learning about a whole box gives a different answer from drawing one coin.

screens.title: Bertrand’s box
screens.prose: Three boxes each hold two coins. You draw one coin and see its colour. We will find what that tells you about the coin still hidden in the box.

state.caption: Gold coins are marked G, silver coins S

screens.prose: Box GG holds two gold coins, box SS two silver, and box GS one of each. You pick a box at random and draw one of its coins without looking inside. The coin is gold.
screens.question: Which box did the gold coin most likely come from?

options.why: You favoured the box with both colours. It gives gold only half the time, while GG gives gold every time.

options.text: GG and GS are equally likely
options.why: You counted boxes, not coins. GG hands you gold every time, GS only half the time.

hints.text: If you picked box GS, how often would you draw gold?
Box GG gives gold every time.
GG gives gold with chance 1, GS with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. So a gold coin points to GG twice as strongly.

feedback.correct: A gold draw is twice as likely from GG as from GS.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how often each box would hand you a gold coin.

explain.text: Box GG produces a gold coin every time, box GS only half the time. So seeing gold favours GG. Next we put a number on it by counting coins.

screens.prose: Each of the six coins is equally likely to be the one you drew: a box with chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$, then a coin with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Each coin has chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

state.caption: Six coins, each drawn with chance 1/6

screens.question: Tap every coin that could be the gold coin you drew.

hints.text: How many gold coins are there in all?
Box GG holds two of them.
Three coins are gold: two in box GG and one in box GS.

feedback.correct: Three gold coins, each equally likely to be the one drawn.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap every gold coin, and only gold coins.

byKey.per-box: You tapped one gold coin in box GG. Both of its coins are gold, and either could be the one you drew.
byKey.per-box-2: You tapped one gold coin in box GG. Both of its coins are gold, and either could be the one you drew.
byKey.b1: That coin is silver. You drew a gold one.
byKey.b2: That coin is silver. You drew a gold one.
byKey.c2: That coin is silver. You drew a gold one.

explain.text: You tapped the three gold coins. Each was equally likely to be drawn, so after seeing gold each has chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$. The news ruled out the three silver coins.

screens.prose: You narrowed the draw to three equally likely gold coins. Each has a partner: the other coin in the same box.

state.caption: Three gold coins could be the one you drew

screens.question: Tap the gold coins whose partner is also gold.

hints.text: What is the partner of the gold coin in box GS?
Box GG's two gold coins are each other's partners.
Both gold coins in GG have a gold partner. The gold coin in GS has a silver one.

feedback.correct: Two of the three gold coins have a gold partner.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each gold coin, look at the other coin in its box.

byKey.all-gold: You tapped every gold coin. The gold coin in box GS has a silver partner.
byKey.c1: The gold coin in box GS has a silver partner.
byKey.b1: That coin is silver, so it cannot be the coin you drew.
byKey.b2: That coin is silver, so it cannot be the coin you drew.
byKey.c2: That coin is silver, so it cannot be the coin you drew.

explain.text: Two of the three equally likely gold coins have a gold partner. So $P(\text{other is gold} \mid \text{drew gold}) = \tfrac{2}{3}$. We counted coins, not boxes: each coin is one equally likely outcome.

screens.prose: The same puzzle as a tree. First the box, each $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Then the coin you draw, given the box. The other coin is gold exactly when the box is GG.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{GG} \mid \text{drew gold})$?

widget.label: Chance the box is GG
widget.accept: Any form equal to $\tfrac{2}{3}$, or a decimal that rounds to 0.67.

hints.text: Which leaves end in a gold coin?
Two paths end in gold: $\tfrac{1}{3}$ through GG and $\tfrac{1}{6}$ through GS.
Divide the GG path by the total: $\dfrac{1/3}{1/3 + 1/6}$.

feedback.correct: The GG path is twice as likely as the GS path.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the paths that end in gold, then take the GG share.

byKey.half: You gave the GG and GS paths equal weight. The GS path also needs a gold coin out of two, so it is half as likely.
byKey.prior: That is the GG path on its own, or the chance before the draw. Divide by the chance of gold, $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

explain.text: Two paths end in gold: $\tfrac{1}{3}$ through GG and $\tfrac{1}{6}$ through GS, together $\tfrac{1}{2}$. So $P(\text{GG} \mid \text{gold}) = \dfrac{1/3}{1/2} = \tfrac{2}{3}$, matching your count of coins.

screens.prose: A fourth box joins: a second GS box. Each of the four boxes now has chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$. You draw a gold coin again.
screens.question: Now what is the chance the other coin is gold?

widget.label: Chance the other coin is gold

hints.text: How many gold coins are there now, and how many have a gold partner?
Gold paths: $\tfrac{1}{4}$ through GG and $\tfrac{1}{8}$ through each GS box.
$\dfrac{1/4}{1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. In coins: 4 gold, 2 with a gold partner.

feedback.correct: The extra GS box adds a gold coin with a silver partner.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every path that ends in gold, then take the GG share.

byKey.old: You kept the old answer. The second GS box adds a gold coin whose partner is silver.
byKey.boxes: You counted boxes: GG is one of three boxes that hold gold. Count gold coins instead.

explain.text: Now there are four gold coins: two in GG and one in each GS box. Two of the four have a gold partner, so the chance is $\tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. The tree agrees: $\dfrac{1/4}{1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

screens.prose: Back to three boxes. A friend argues: “The gold coin came from GG or GS. Each box had chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so the other coin is gold with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.”
screens.question: What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: Box GG was twice as likely to hand you gold, so the gold coin is evidence for it
Nothing: two boxes are left, so it is $\tfrac{1}{2}$
options.why: You accepted “GG or GS, so 50:50”. The boxes are equally likely before the draw, not after it.

options.text: Box SS should still count, so it is $\tfrac{1}{3}$
options.why: You kept box SS in play. It holds no gold, so the draw rules it out.

options.text: Box GS is likelier, because it has both colours
options.why: You favoured the mixed box. It gives gold only half the time, so the draw counts against it.

hints.text: How likely is a gold draw from GG? From GS?
Three gold coins could have been drawn, and two of them sit in GG.
The likelihood ratio is $1 : \tfrac{1}{2}$, so the odds of GG to GS move from $1:1$ to $2:1$.

feedback.correct: Equal boxes before the draw, but the draw favours GG two to one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how likely the gold coin was from each box.

byKey.fifty: You accepted “GG or GS, so 50:50”. That counts boxes. Count gold coins: two of the three sit in GG.

explain.text: The draw favours GG: it gives gold with chance 1, and GS with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. The odds of GG to GS move from $1:1$ to $2:1$, so $P(\text{GG}) = \tfrac{2}{3}$. Counting boxes ignores how the gold coin came to be seen.

screens.title: Looking instead of drawing
screens.prose: New rules. You pick a box at random but draw nothing. Instead a clerk looks inside and tells you: “This box holds at least one gold coin.”

state.caption: The clerk looks at the whole box

screens.question: What is the chance the box is GG?

hints.text: Which boxes fit the clerk's statement?
Boxes GG and GS both hold a gold coin.
The clerk would say this for GG and for GS alike. Each was $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so each is now $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

feedback.correct: The clerk's news is equally likely from GG and GS.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which boxes the clerk's statement fits, and how often it would be said for each.

byKey.coins: You counted gold coins, as if one had been drawn. The clerk reports on the whole box, so GG and GS fit equally.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before the clerk spoke. Box SS is now ruled out.

explain.text: The clerk says the same thing for GG as for GS, so the likelihood ratio is 1 and the two stay equal at $\tfrac{1}{2}$. A drawn coin carried more, because GG makes a gold draw more likely. How you learn “gold” changes the answer.

screens.prose: Rebuild the drawn-coin answer in odds form, the tool from level 2. Compare GG with GS, since the gold coin rules out SS.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Before the draw, the odds of GG to GS are $1 : 1$, since each box has chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$
After the draw, the odds of GG to GS are $2 : 1$
So $P(\text{GG} \mid \text{gold}) = \dfrac{2}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, turning odds into a probability

hints.text: Odds form starts from the odds before any evidence.
The likelihood ratio multiplies the prior odds.
Prior odds, then multiply by the likelihood ratio, then the posterior odds, then the probability.

feedback.correct: Prior odds times likelihood ratio gives posterior odds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the odds before the draw.

byKey.lr: You need odds to multiply first. Start with the odds before the draw.
byKey.post: The posterior odds come from multiplying, so the ratio comes before them.
byKey.prob: Turning odds into a probability is the last step.

explain.text: The draw doubles the odds for GG, because GG gives gold twice as often as GS. Odds of $2:1$ mean $\tfrac{2}{3}$. A clerk's report that is equally likely from both boxes has ratio 1 and leaves the odds at $1:1$.

screens.prose: A fund family runs 10 funds, each with two share classes. In 3 funds both classes had a great year, in 2 only one class did, and in 5 neither did. A newsletter picks one share class at random and reports: “a great year”.
screens.question: What is the chance the other class of the same fund also had a great year?

widget.label: Chance the sister class had a great year

hints.text: How many share classes had a great year?
Both-great funds give $3 \times 2 = 6$ great classes, and the one-great funds give 2.
Eight great classes, and six of them sit in a fund whose other class was also great.

feedback.correct: Six of the eight great classes have a great sister class.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The newsletter picked a class, so count great classes, not funds.

byKey.funds: You counted funds: 3 of the 5 funds with a great class. The newsletter picked a class, so count classes.
byKey.half: You treated the fund as equally likely to be a both-great or a one-great fund. A both-great fund is twice as likely to be reported.
byKey.all: That is the share of all funds where both classes were great. The report rules out the funds with no great class.

explain.text: There are 8 great classes: 6 in both-great funds and 2 in one-great funds. The reported class is equally likely to be any of the 8, and 6 of them have a great sister: $\tfrac{6}{8} = \tfrac{3}{4}$. Counting funds gives $\tfrac{3}{5}$, the box-counting mistake.

ideas: When a coin is drawn at random, each coin is an equally likely outcome: count coins, not boxes.
Box GG hands you gold twice as often as box GS, so a gold draw moves the odds from $1:1$ to $2:1$: the answer is $\tfrac{2}{3}$.
A report about the whole box, such as “it holds some gold”, fits GG and GS equally and gives $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

formula.name: Odds form for the boxes
formula.note: Posterior odds are prior odds times the likelihood ratio.

summary.trap: “It is GG or GS, so 50:50” counts boxes. The draw is evidence, and GG produces it twice as often.

quiz.prose: Three cards: one red on both sides, one blue on both sides, one red on one side and blue on the other. A card is picked at random and laid down with a random side up. The top is red.
quiz.question: What is the chance the bottom is red too?

options.why: You counted cards: red-red or red-blue. Count red faces instead: three, and two have a red back.
That is the chance of the red-red card before you saw a face. A red face makes it likelier.

feedback.correct: Two of the three red faces have a red back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the red faces, then those with a red back.

explain.text: Three faces are red: two on the red-red card and one on the red-blue card. Each is equally likely to be on top. Two have a red back, so the chance is $\tfrac{2}{3}$.

quiz.prose: Boxes GG, SS and GS. You pick a box at random and draw one coin from it.
quiz.question: Before you look, what is the chance the coin is gold?

options.why: You counted the box with only gold coins. Box GS can also give gold.
You counted boxes that hold gold. Box GS gives gold only half the time.

feedback.correct: Three of the six equally likely coins are gold.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count gold coins among all six.

explain.text: Each of the six coins is drawn with chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$, and three are gold. So the chance is $\tfrac{3}{6} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. In tree form: $\tfrac{1}{3} \cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{3} \cdot 0 + \tfrac{1}{3} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

quiz.prose: Two boxes: one holds three gold coins, the other one gold and two silver. You pick a box at random, draw a coin, and it is gold.
quiz.question: What is the chance you picked the all-gold box?

options.why: You counted boxes. The all-gold box gives gold every time, the other only a third of the time.
You reused the answer from Bertrand's box. Here the gold coins split 3 to 1.
That is the chance you picked the mixed box. The question asks for the all-gold box.

feedback.correct: Three of the four gold coins sit in the all-gold box.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count gold coins in each box.

explain.text: There are four gold coins, three of them in the all-gold box. Each coin was equally likely to be drawn, so the chance is $\tfrac{3}{4}$. In odds: $1:1$ times a likelihood ratio of $1 : \tfrac{1}{3}$ gives $3:1$.

quiz.prose: The three cards again: red-red, blue-blue, red-blue. A dealer picks one at random, looks at both sides, and says: “This card has at least one red side.”
quiz.question: What is the chance it is the red-red card?

options.why: You counted red faces, as if one were shown at random. The dealer's statement is equally likely for both cards with red.
That is the chance before the dealer spoke. The blue-blue card is ruled out.

feedback.correct: The statement fits red-red and red-blue equally.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which cards the dealer's statement fits.

explain.text: The dealer would say the same for red-red and red-blue, so both stay equally likely: $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each. A face shown at random would have favoured red-red. The answer depends on how you learnt about the red.
